title: Humans Watched This Supernova Explode Nearly a Millennium Ago. Now You Can See It in High Definition
author: Jorge Garay
text:
Astronomers have obtained the most detailed image to date of the Pa 30 nebula, the remnants of a supernova famous for having likely been observed and documented from Earth during the Middle Ages. Now, the new photograph reveals structures that had long gone unnoticed.Previous images of the explosion’s remnants had also captured a sphere of long, filament-like strands of matter that collectively resemble fireworks or a dandelion. The new observations, made with the Gemini North telescope in Hawaii, revealed about 10 times more structures than any previous glimpses of the supernova remnant. With this resolution, researchers can now see that these filaments are not continuous as they had previously appeared. Instead, they’re shaped more like beads on a string, made up of pearl-like knots of gas of relatively uniform size.WIRED's Guide to How the Universe WorksYour weekly roundup of the best stories on health care, the climate crisis, new scientific discoveries, and more.These “cosmic pearls” are, in fact, enormous. According to the study published in The Astrophysical Journal, each bead measures about four light-days in diameter. “The planetary region of our solar system could fit in each knot about 10 times with room to spare,” Ilaria Caiazzo, a coauthor of the study, said in a press release. “The knots are quite strikingly uniform. We are excited to try to model them.”Featured VideoA Dead Star May Be Behind These Mysterious Radio SignalsHow exactly the pearls formed is not yet entirely clear, though it’s assumed they are concentrations of material ejected during the explosion. What’s strange, however, is their regularity. In the aftermath of a supernova, astronomers expected to find much more oddly shaped accumulations, but the knots are similar in size and appear aligned along the filaments. This peculiar order is a new feature that could help researchers gain a deeper understanding of stellar death.This image, obtained with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph, shows that the ejecta from the remnant—with its unmistakable fireworks-like shape—form a cascading structure resembling a knot.

Instead, it’s considered a “zombie star.” Typically, a thermonuclear supernova is the violent death of a star, which is completely destroyed in the explosion. But in rare cases, part of the star may survive, and scientists do not yet fully understand how or why this happens. The unusual structures of Pa 30 could help astronomers reconstruct more precisely how these kinds of detonations occur and how zombie stars can live on afterward.All of this has been discovered because scientists seem to have a bit of a crush on Pa 30. Few astronomical structures connect modern observation so directly with human accounts from more than eight centuries ago. The nebula matches the records left by Chinese and Japanese astronomers in 1181, who described the appearance of a new star in the sky that remained visible for several months. At the time, it was impossible to know that they were witnessing the aftermath of a massive stellar explosion. Centuries later, scientists linked that event to the supernova that gave rise to Pa 30.This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.
